text: Technical documentation review, product Occlivue LVO. The manufacturer, Caldera Imaging GmbH, claims class IIb; the reviewer agrees. The software runs a convolutional network over non-contrast head CT and CT angiography series to flag suspected large-vessel occlusion and to notify the on-call interventional team through the PACS worklist. Intended users are radiologists and stroke physicians; no output is shown to patients. Training used 41,000 anonymised scans from nine European hospitals, and the manufacturer retained patient sex, age and recorded ethnicity alongside the imaging to measure and correct sensitivity gaps between subgroups. Clinical evaluation report accepted. Open item: the alert latency budget in the risk file is 90 seconds, but bench testing shows 140 seconds on the smallest supported server.
rationale: Class IIb is stated. Imaging and recorded ethnicity were retained to measure and correct subgroup sensitivity gaps, so special-category data is processed for bias correction. Output goes to clinicians only, so no direct interaction with persons.

text: 3.2 Intended purpose. RhythmLedger analyses continuous single-lead ECG recorded by the compatible adhesive patch worn by adult outpatients for up to 14 days. A trained classifier labels each episode as atrial fibrillation, supraventricular tachycardia, pause or artefact and compiles a report for the prescribing cardiologist. 3.3 Contraindications. Not for patients with implanted pacemakers or for in-hospital monitoring of unstable patients. 3.4 Warnings. The software does not raise real-time alarms; episodes are reviewed at the end of the wear period. Reports must be confirmed by a qualified clinician before any change in anticoagulation. 3.5 Residual risk. A missed episode of atrial fibrillation may delay the start of treatment. Report any suspected malfunction to Vektorlabs Medical AB and to your national competent authority.
rationale: A trained classifier that labels arrhythmia episodes to inform a cardiologist's diagnostic and treatment decisions is a medical device; class left implicit, IIa (diagnostic information, no immediate danger). No training-data, conversational or generative claims in the text.

text: Summary of safety and clinical performance (draft). Device: ContourPilot RT, class IIb, manufacturer Halden Oncology Systems. ContourPilot segments organs at risk and gross tumour volume on planning CT for head-and-neck and prostate radiotherapy, and writes a narrative planning note describing the delineated structures, margins and any regions where the segmentation confidence was low. The dosimetrist edits both the contours and the note before approval by the radiation oncologist. The segmentation models were trained on 6,200 planning CTs with linked diagnosis codes, tumour stage and treatment outcomes; performance was then compared across age bands and between male and female patients, and the training set was rebalanced where Dice scores diverged. A systematic contouring error that survives review could lead to under-dosing the target or over-dosing the spinal cord.
rationale: Class IIb stated. The device writes a narrative planning note, i.e. generated text. Training used CTs with diagnosis codes and outcomes and the set was rebalanced after subgroup comparison, so health data was used to train and debias.

text: Protocol SEPSIS-WATCH-02, synopsis. Design: prospective, multicentre, stepped-wedge trial in 14 intensive care units. Intervention: Sepsaro, a gradient-boosted model that recomputes a six-hour sepsis probability every fifteen minutes from vital signs, laboratory results, ventilator parameters and medication orders drawn from the electronic record, and pushes a bedside alert when the probability crosses a unit-configurable threshold. Comparator: standard qSOFA screening by nursing staff. Primary endpoint: time from first physiological deterioration to antibiotic administration. Secondary endpoints: 28-day mortality, false alert rate per bed-day. The model was developed on retrospective records from 92,000 ICU admissions, and the sponsor stratified calibration by sex, age and documented chronic conditions to identify and reduce subgroups with inferior recall. Sponsor: Northreach Critical Care Analytics. Enrolment target: 8,400 patients.
rationale: A learned model that monitors ICU patients and alerts on impending sepsis is a medical device; class implicit, IIb (monitoring of vital physiological processes where variation is immediately dangerous). Calibration was stratified by documented chronic conditions to reduce weak subgroups, so health data was used to debias.

text: Meet Naelith. Point your phone at a mole, and in under ten seconds Naelith tells you whether it looks like something a dermatologist should see this month, or whether it can wait for your next routine check. Our image model was built with dermatologists from four university clinics and reads colour, border, asymmetry and texture at once. Not sure how to take the photo? Ask Mo, the in-app assistant: it talks you through lighting, distance and framing, and answers questions about what the result means. Naelith is a CE-marked medical device available in 11 EU countries. It is not a replacement for a clinical examination, and any lesion that bleeds, grows or changes colour should be shown to a doctor regardless of the result.
rationale: An image model telling users whether a lesion needs a dermatologist is a diagnostic-triage medical device; class implicit, IIa. Mo is a conversational assistant that talks to the user, so the system interacts directly with persons. No training-data detail is given.

text: Oslo, 4 March — Fjordmind AS today announced that Duskward, its prescription digital therapy for mild-to-moderate depression, has received CE certification as a class IIa medical device. Duskward delivers an eight-week programme of behavioural activation and cognitive restructuring through a conversational companion that adapts each session to what the user wrote the day before, composing new reflection prompts and summaries rather than selecting them from a fixed library. Weekly PHQ-9 trends are shared with the prescribing clinician. 'Patients told us a script feels like a script,' said CEO Ingrid Solvang. 'Duskward listens and writes back.' A randomised trial of 412 participants showed a mean PHQ-9 reduction of 5.1 points against 2.3 in the waitlist arm. Duskward will be available through Norwegian and German prescribers from June.
rationale: Class IIa stated. The therapy is delivered by a conversational companion (interacts with persons) that composes new prompts and summaries rather than picking from a library (generated text).

text: Lot 3 — Automated diabetic eye screening. The contracting authority, Westmarch Regional Health Board, seeks a software service that reads two-field fundus photographs captured at 46 community optometry sites and returns, without clinician review, one of three outcomes: no referable retinopathy (recall in twelve months), referable retinopathy (ophthalmology appointment within four weeks), or ungradable image (repeat capture). The learned grading model shall achieve sensitivity of at least 95% for referable disease on the authority's held-out set of 3,000 graded image pairs. Bidders shall supply the EU declaration of conformity and the certificate issued by their notified body, the full instructions for use, and a description of how image quality failures are detected. Service availability of 99.5% during clinic hours is a mandatory requirement.
rationale: A learned grading model that autonomously decides referral for diabetic retinopathy is a diagnostic medical device requiring a notified-body certificate; class implicit, IIa. Nothing in the text indicates conversational, generative or bias-correction processing by the provider.

text: Background: Prostate biopsy grading shows substantial inter-observer variation. Methods: We evaluated GleasonGrid, a commercially available whole-slide image classifier that outlines tumour regions and proposes a Gleason grade group for each core, in routine sign-out at three pathology departments over nine months (11,804 cores). Pathologists saw the overlay before recording their own grade. The vendor reports that the model was trained on 48,000 cores with linked prostatectomy outcomes and that grade concordance was audited separately for patients over 75 and for Black patients, with additional cases added where agreement lagged. Results: Concordance with the central reference panel rose from 71.2% to 83.6%; median reporting time fell by 4 minutes per case. Two cores with cribriform pattern were under-graded by the software and corrected by the reporting pathologist. Conclusion: Overlay-assisted grading improved agreement with no missed carcinoma.
rationale: Software grading prostate biopsy tissue is an in vitro diagnostic under IVDR 2017/746, class C (Annex VIII Rule 3), which needs a notified body; recorded as IIb under the brief's IVDR mapping (C to IIb). Concordance audited for Black patients, with cases added where agreement lagged, is special-category data processed for bias correction.

text: Somnary — the prescribed sleep programme. Problem: 1 in 10 European adults has chronic insomnia; CBT-I is first-line therapy but waiting lists run to nine months. Product: a twelve-week app delivering CBT-I in which a reinforcement-learning policy sets each patient's weekly sleep window from their diary and wearable data, and an in-app coach answers questions and nudges adherence in natural language. Regulatory: CE certificate as a class IIa medical device obtained Q2; reimbursement dossier filed in Germany and France. Traction: 3,100 prescriptions in pilot clinics, 68% completion, mean sleep-efficiency gain of 14 points. Business model: EUR 290 per prescription, paid by statutory insurers. Team: founders from sleep medicine and reinforcement learning. Ask: EUR 6M Series A to fund the French launch and a paediatric indication.
rationale: Class IIa stated. The reinforcement-learning policy is the AI component; the in-app coach that answers questions in natural language interacts directly with persons. No generated media or bias-correction claim.

text: @regulatory-team quick one before the Friday call with the notified body. Reminder of what AcuityQ actually does, since the auditor asked: at registration in the emergency department it takes the triage nurse's vitals, chief complaint free text and age, runs them through our trained risk model and assigns a priority band 1–5 plus a predicted probability of ICU admission within 24 hours. Band drives who gets seen first. Nurses can override, and about 9% of bands are changed manually. We never show anything to the patient. Also the auditor wants the usability file for the override button and the post-market plan for alert fatigue. Can someone from clinical confirm the rate of band-1 patients who were actually admitted to ICU in the Antwerp pilot? Need it by Thursday, thanks.
rationale: A trained model assigning emergency-department priority bands and predicting ICU admission is a medical device under notified-body review; class implicit, IIa. It is also emergency patient triage (essential services) and evaluates each patient's health outlook, so profiling is set. Both routes apply; the MDR route determines the tier.

text: Subject: Framework call-off — CardioCue licence for the Northern dispatch centre. Dear Ms Varga, following the evaluation panel, we intend to call off 40 operator seats of CardioCue from the framework. For the file, please confirm the following in writing: that CardioCue listens to the live audio of incoming emergency calls and, using a speech model trained on 180,000 recorded calls matched to ambulance and hospital outcome records, raises an on-screen prompt when the caller's description and background sounds suggest out-of-hospital cardiac arrest; that the dispatcher remains free to ignore the prompt; that the product carries CE marking as a class IIa medical device under your certificate number; and that no call audio leaves our tenancy. We also require the false-positive rate from the Dutch pilot. Kind regards, Procurement Officer, Regional Emergency Medical Services.
rationale: Class IIa stated. Evaluating live emergency calls for dispatch is the emergency-call evaluation area (essential services). Training on calls matched to outcome records uses health data, but no bias-detection purpose is described, so special-category data stays false. It listens but does not converse, so no direct interaction.

text: Posted in Nursing Informatics > Emergency. Has anyone else worked with the TriageTalk kiosk? Our ED put two of them by the entrance in September. Walk-in patients type or speak their complaint, the thing asks follow-up questions like a nurse would (pain scale, duration, meds), and then prints a ticket with a priority colour that feeds our tracking board. The label on the back says class IIa, CE marked, made by Avenir Santé Numérique. Mostly I like it, the waiting room is calmer and the red tickets have all been real so far. But twice it gave a green to older patients with vague chest discomfort, and we caught both at the desk. Is anyone collecting override data? I want to bring numbers to our quality meeting rather than anecdotes.
rationale: Class IIa stated on the label. The kiosk converses with patients (interacts with persons) and assigns emergency priority, so the triage area and profiling of each patient's urgency are also set. MDR route determines the tier.

text: Clinical evaluation summary — Ictavane wrist sensor and companion software, class IIb, Brimstone Neurotech Ltd. Intended purpose: to forecast the probability of a generalised tonic-clonic seizure in the following 60 minutes for adults with drug-resistant epilepsy, from electrodermal activity, heart-rate variability and accelerometry, and to alert the patient and a nominated carer. The recurrent network underlying the forecast was trained on 2,900 patient-months of wearable data with video-EEG confirmed seizure timestamps; the dataset was stratified by epilepsy syndrome, sex and anti-seizure medication load to check that sensitivity did not fall below 80% in any stratum. Pivotal study: 214 participants, sensitivity 86%, one false alarm per 3.2 days. A missed forecast removes the opportunity to reach a safe position before a seizure; this residual risk is disclosed in the patient leaflet.
rationale: Class IIb stated. Training data were wearable traces with confirmed seizure timestamps, stratified by syndrome and medication load to check subgroup sensitivity, so health data was used for training and bias testing. Alerts are notifications, not a conversation.

text: Section 2 — Description. VentiGuide is a software option for the Aerolux 700 intensive-care ventilator. In Advisory mode it displays a recommended pressure-support level and FiO2 derived from a learned model of the patient's tidal volume, respiratory rate, end-tidal CO2 and oxygen saturation over the preceding thirty minutes. In Assist mode it applies the recommended pressure-support change automatically within the limits set by the clinician, who is notified of every adjustment. Section 4 — Warnings. Assist mode must not be used in patients with unstable haemodynamics or during spontaneous breathing trials. Never leave a patient in Assist mode without an active apnoea backup. Section 7 — Known limitations. The model was not validated in paediatric patients or in patients with a tracheostomy cuff leak above 15%. Manufacturer: Aerolux Medical Systems S.p.A.
rationale: A learned model that adjusts ventilator settings on ICU patients is software driving an active therapeutic device; class implicit, IIb. No patient-facing conversation, generated content or bias-correction statement.

text: Study title: Diagnostic accuracy of FetalSense automated cardiotocograph interpretation in intrapartum care. Setting: eight maternity units, 6,000 labours. The investigational software receives the live fetal heart-rate and uterine-contraction traces from bedside monitors and, using a sequence model, classifies each 30-minute window as normal, suspicious or pathological and signals to the midwife when a pathological pattern persists. Reference standard: blinded panel of three obstetricians. Development data: 410,000 hours of traces with neonatal outcomes from the manufacturer's partner hospitals; the manufacturer reports that cases were weighted by maternal body-mass index, parity and self-reported ethnicity after an early analysis found lower sensitivity in the highest BMI group. Primary outcome: sensitivity and specificity for pathological traces preceding umbilical artery pH below 7.05. Sponsor: Cradlewave Diagnostics Oy.
rationale: A sequence model interpreting live intrapartum CTG and signalling pathological patterns monitors a vital process where variation is immediately dangerous; class implicit, IIb. Cases were re-weighted by BMI, parity and ethnicity after a subgroup sensitivity gap, so health and ethnicity data were used to debias.

text: GlucoHelm for intensive care. Tight glycaemic control without the spreadsheet. GlucoHelm reads each point-of-care glucose value as it is entered, considers the patient's insulin infusion history, nutrition rate and renal function, and proposes the next infusion rate and the time of the next check. Nurses confirm or edit the proposal; every proposal and every edit is logged. Built by intensivists: the dosing model learned from 1.4 million glucose–insulin pairs and is re-tuned for your unit's protocol during onboarding. Certified: CE marked, class III, certificate issued by our notified body in 2025. Proven: hypoglycaemic events below 2.2 mmol/L fell 41% in a two-centre comparison. Compatible with the major point-of-care meters and HL7 feeds. Book a demo or download the clinical summary.
rationale: Class III stated. A learned dosing model proposing insulin infusion rates for ICU patients. The glucose–insulin training pairs are described as data points, not as a bias-correction use of health data, so special-category data is left false; no conversation or generated media.

text: Specification 4.1 — Emergency department flow prediction. The Trust requires a software service that, for each patient at the point of arrival, predicts the likely waiting time, the probability of admission and a recommended order of assessment, using the registration record, arrival mode, time of day and departmental occupancy. The supplier has confirmed that the service is marketed as an operational planning tool and is not CE marked as a medical device; the Trust accepts this positioning for the purpose of this lot. The recommended order is displayed on the charge nurse's board and may be amended at any time. The supplier shall provide monthly reports on the accuracy of the admission prediction by age band and shall support integration with the Trust's patient administration system within twelve weeks of award.
rationale: Recommending the order in which emergency patients are assessed is emergency patient triage (essential services). The service is explicitly not a medical device. It predicts each person's admission probability, so profiling is set; no narrow-task exception is claimed.

text: Lisbon — Linha Viva Tecnologia announced today that the national emergency number operator will deploy Prioridade, its call-urgency engine, across all four regional dispatch centres by autumn. Prioridade listens alongside the call-taker, transcribes the conversation and estimates, as the call unfolds, whether the incident needs an advanced life-support ambulance, a basic ambulance or telephone advice, and presents its estimate next to the dispatcher's own protocol questions. The engine was trained on 2.3 million historical calls joined to the patient's later hospital diagnosis and survival. 'The dispatcher stays in command; Prioridade simply reads the call faster,' said founder Teresa Almada. Linha Viva states that the product is not a medical device and has not been CE marked as one. A twelve-month evaluation in the Algarve centre reported a nine percent reduction in over-triage of advanced units.
rationale: Evaluating and classifying emergency calls for dispatch is the essential-services area; the vendor states it is not a medical device. Training joined calls to hospital diagnosis and survival, but nothing says that data was used to detect or correct bias, so special-category data stays false. It estimates each caller's clinical urgency, which is profiling; no exception is claimed.

text: Subject: Clarification on the CarePath eligibility scoring module. Dear supplier, thank you for the demonstration to the Long-Term Care Directorate yesterday. Before we proceed to contract, please confirm our understanding. CarePath ingests each application for the regional home-care subsidy — functional assessment scores, GP letters, household income and the applicant's hospital-admission history — and produces an eligibility recommendation with a care-hours band, trained on the Directorate's decisions from 2016 to 2024. Assessors see the recommendation before meeting the applicant and record a reason whenever they depart from it. We also need the error analysis by applicant age group, confirmation that recommendations are recalculated when new medical documents arrive, and the data processing agreement in our template. Regards, Head of Procurement, Regional Social Affairs Authority.
rationale: Recommending eligibility and care-hours for a public home-care subsidy is public-benefit eligibility (essential services). It evaluates each applicant's health and circumstances, so profiling is set, and the recommendation shapes the decision rather than performing a narrow or preparatory task.

text: Quillbeck Underwriting — pricing health cover from how people actually live. Thesis: traditional health-insurance underwriting relies on a questionnaire and age. Product: Quillbeck plugs into insurers' quote flows and, with consent, pulls 90 days of step count, resting heart rate and sleep from the applicant's wearable, together with declared conditions and prescription history, to produce an individual risk score and a premium adjustment within seconds. The scoring model was trained on claims and wearable histories of 1.1 million policyholders from two partner insurers, including diagnosis codes, and is monitored for drift quarterly. Traction: live with three insurers in Spain and Poland; EUR 2.1M ARR. Why now: consumer wearables have reached 38% penetration in our target markets. Ask: EUR 9M to enter the German market and add a life-insurance pricing module.
rationale: Risk scoring and premium adjustment for health insurance is the essential-services area. An individual risk score from health and behaviour data is profiling. Training on claims histories with diagnosis codes and drift monitoring are not a bias-detection use of health data, so special-category data stays false. Not a medical device.

text: #people-ops — Hey all, update on Bandsift. Since Monday every application for the band 5 nursing posts goes through the vendor's ranking model before the recruiter sees it. It scores the CV, the free-text supporting statement and the online situational-judgement test and puts candidates in three piles: interview, hold, decline. Recruiters can move anyone between piles, but by default only the top pile gets a call. Vendor says the model was trained on our last six years of hiring decisions plus one-year retention. Two things I need: (1) legal wants the candidate privacy notice updated this week; (2) can someone pull the pile distribution by age and gender from the dashboard for the equality impact assessment? We promised the union a first look in two weeks.
rationale: Ranking and filtering job applications for nursing posts is the employment area. Scoring each candidate's statement and test is profiling. No medical purpose, no exception claimed. The training data are hiring decisions, not health data.

text: OpMetric — objective surgical skill, every case. OpMetric's computer-vision engine analyses the laparoscopic video of each procedure and scores the operating surgeon on instrument economy, bimanual dexterity, tissue handling and idle time, then benchmarks the score against peers performing the same procedure. Hospital directors receive quarterly dashboards per surgeon; department chairs use OpMetric scores in annual appraisal and in granting or renewing operating privileges. Surgeons see their own trend line and short clips of their best and weakest moments. OpMetric is a quality and workforce tool: it does not assist in the procedure, makes no claim about patient outcomes and is not a medical device. Trusted by 27 hospitals across the Benelux. Request access for your surgical department.
rationale: Scoring surgeons for appraisal and operating privileges is evaluating work performance (employment area) and profiles each surgeon. The page states it is not a medical device. Video analysis of technique is not emotion recognition or biometric categorisation.

text: Synopsis — observational feasibility study of MoodMirror in a dementia care unit. MoodMirror, placed on the EU market as a class IIa medical device by Serenwood Health, uses ceiling cameras and a facial-expression and vocal-tone model to classify each resident's emotional state (calm, anxious, agitated, in pain) every ten seconds and to alert care staff by pager when distress persists beyond two minutes. Objective: to compare time-to-staff-response for distress episodes with and without the alerts in 36 residents over twelve weeks. Secondary objectives: staff acceptance, false-alert rate, and agreement between model output and nurse-rated PAINAD scores. Ethical note: residents' representatives give written consent; cameras are disabled in bathrooms. Sponsor's statement: the device is intended to support care staff and makes no therapeutic recommendation.
rationale: Emotion recognition from face and voice in a care setting is the biometrics area and sets the emotion flag; it is for medical/care purposes, so not a prohibited practice. Monitoring residents to inform care decisions is MDR Rule 11 class IIa, as the text states, so the device route makes it high-risk under Art. 6(1). Classifying each resident's state is profiling.

text: Lot 1 — Perimeter and corridor identification. The University Hospital of Sankt Alder invites tenders for a video analytics platform that compares faces captured by the 212 existing corridor and entrance cameras against a hospital-managed reference list of persons subject to exclusion orders, missing in-patients and staff authorised for restricted wards, and alerts the security desk with a match score within three seconds. The platform shall operate on live streams without any action by the person being identified. Mandatory: on-premise processing, deletion of non-matching face templates within 24 hours, audit log of every match reviewed by security staff, and documented accuracy by age, sex and skin tone. The hospital is a private foundation and the system will not be operated by or for police forces. Contract term four years.
rationale: Matching faces from corridor cameras against a reference list at a distance, without the person's involvement, is remote biometric identification (biometrics area). It is a private hospital, not law enforcement in public spaces, so not prohibited. It identifies rather than evaluates persons, so profiling and emotion flags stay false. Documented accuracy by skin tone means biometric data is processed to detect disparities, so special-category data is set. Not a medical device.

text: Caseworkers forum — thread: 'FrailSort, anyone?' Our regional office switched on FrailSort last month for the disability-living allowance queue. It doesn't decide anything; the vendor keeps saying it only does the preparatory sorting so that we open the files in a sensible order. What it actually does is read the medical certificates and the applicant's hospital discharge letters, estimate how likely each person is to meet the frailty threshold, and rank the queue by that estimate. Likely approvals float to the top so they get paid faster, which is nice. But the people it ranks low wait longer, and I have started seeing the estimate before I have read anything myself, which I don't love. Our decision is still ours, formally. Does anyone have a practice note on this?
rationale: Sorting a public disability-benefit queue is the essential-services area (5(a)). The vendor calls it preparatory, but the per-applicant estimate is shown first and floats likely approvals to the top, so it influences the assessment: no exception. Estimating each applicant's likelihood of meeting a frailty threshold from medical records is also profiling.

text: Title: Pattern detection in nursing performance records at a 900-bed hospital. Background: Line managers complete quarterly performance reviews for 2,400 nursing staff. Methods: We deployed ShiftLens, a text-mining and scoring tool, over three years of completed review forms, incident reports and sickness records. ShiftLens does not write or alter reviews; managers' assessments stand as recorded. It identifies recurring patterns — for example, late-shift clusters of medication errors on a given ward — and additionally assigns each nurse a reliability index that is shown to the manager alongside the next review form. Results: 31 ward-level patterns were surfaced; 14 led to rota changes. Managers consulted the reliability index in 78% of reviews, and nurses in the lowest decile were twice as likely to receive a development plan. Conclusion: Pattern surfacing is feasible; the individual index raises fairness questions we discuss.
rationale: Evaluating nursing staff performance is the employment area (4(b)). The per-nurse reliability index is shown to the manager with the review form and was consulted in most reviews, so it influences the human assessment: no exception. The index is profiling of work performance.

text: Vienna — Corvik Re today released Underwrite Assistant, a large-language-model service for life and private health insurers that reads an applicant's submitted medical records, attending-physician statements and prescription history, extracts the relevant conditions and produces a mortality and morbidity risk class with a written justification for the underwriter. Insurers can configure the service to issue a premium loading automatically for straightforward files. The model was fine-tuned on 600,000 anonymised underwriting files including diagnoses and outcomes contributed by Corvik Re's cedants and is evaluated monthly against senior underwriter decisions. 'Files that took forty minutes now take four,' said Head of Product Markus Hiebl. Underwrite Assistant is offered to insurers in the EU from today; an applicant-facing explanation letter is generated on request.
rationale: Risk classification and premium loading for life and health insurance is the essential-services area; assigning each applicant a risk class from medical records is profiling. The LLM writes justifications and explanation letters (generated text). Fine-tuning on files including diagnoses and monthly accuracy evaluation are not a bias-detection use, so special-category data stays false. Not a medical device.

text: Need urgent care tonight? Start with Vigil. Vigil is the official urgent-care front door of the Vellmark Health Region. Tell Vigil what is wrong in your own words; it asks the questions a triage nurse would ask, and within three minutes tells you whether to call an ambulance, go to the emergency department (and books your arrival slot), see an out-of-hours GP, or treat yourself at home with its instructions. Behind the conversation is a clinical reasoning model trained on 4 million past urgent-care contacts and their outcomes, reviewed by our medical board every quarter. Vigil is CE marked as a class IIa medical device by Vellmark Digital Health. If someone is unconscious, not breathing or bleeding heavily, call 112 immediately instead.
rationale: Urgent-care triage that decides between ambulance, emergency department, GP and self-care is emergency patient triage (essential services, 5(d)) and a medical device that informs therapeutic decisions, class IIa under MDR Rule 11, so the MDR route applies first. Assessing each caller's urgency is profiling; the conversation sets interacts_with_persons.

text: Subject: Order confirmation — ScribeLift licences for the ambulance service. Dear Mr Okafor, we confirm the order of 120 ScribeLift tablet licences. As discussed, ScribeLift will be used by crews to photograph the handwritten patient report form at the end of each call; the handwriting-recognition model converts the form into structured fields (times, observations, drugs given) and uploads them to the control-room record. It performs no assessment of the patient, does not rank or prioritise calls or crews, and runs only after the handover is complete. Fields below the confidence threshold are highlighted for the crew to correct on the tablet. Please schedule the installation for the first week of May and send the offline-mode documentation requested by our IT security officer. Regards, Fleet and Equipment Manager, County Ambulance Service.
rationale: Converts handwritten patient report forms to structured fields after handover; it assesses, ranks and prioritises no one. The system performs none of the uses Annex III lists for its sector, so no Annex III area is set and the Art. 6(3) exception does not arise. No conversation or generated content, so minimal.

text: Requirement 2.4 — Live transcription for emergency call handling. The contracting authority operates the 112 answering centre for the eastern province and requires a speech-recognition service that produces a live, scrolling transcript of each incoming call on the call-taker's second screen, in the three regional languages, with speaker separation between caller and operator. The service shall not interpret, score or summarise the call, shall not propose a dispatch category and shall not alter the order in which calls are handled; the authority's protocol software remains the sole source of priority. Required word error rate: below 12% on the authority's test corpus. Transcripts are stored with the call recording for 90 days and are used afterwards for quality review. Bidders shall document latency, on-premise deployment options and how background noise is handled.
rationale: A speech-to-text transcript for 112 call-takers that, as required, does not evaluate, classify, prioritise or dispatch calls: not a use listed in Annex III point 5(d), so no area and no exception. Transcription is not generated content and the system does not converse, so minimal.

text: Ask Beneo. Applying for a health-cost subsidy in the Lowland Provinces can be confusing, so Beneo is here to help, around the clock, in Dutch, French and English. Beneo answers questions about which documents you need, where to send them, how long the review takes and what the appeal process looks like, drawing on the published regulations and the provincial FAQ. Beneo does not look at your application and cannot tell you whether you will qualify, how much you will receive or when a decision will be made on your file; those answers come only from the subsidy office after a caseworker has reviewed your documents. Everything you type is deleted at the end of the conversation unless you ask Beneo to email you a summary. Beneo is a service of the Provincial Social Affairs Department, built by Civiq Software.
rationale: An applicant-side help assistant that explains documents, deadlines and appeals and never sees or evaluates an application; Annex III 5(a) covers systems used by public authorities to evaluate eligibility. The system performs none of the uses Annex III lists for its sector, so no Annex III area is set and the Art. 6(3) exception does not arise. It answers applicants directly, so interacts_with_persons.

text: #claims-ops: heads up, the DocSorter rollout is finished for the health line. Every incoming attachment on a claim (invoices, prescriptions, discharge letters, random photos of receipts) now gets classified by document type and routed to the right queue, and obvious duplicates get flagged with a link to the earlier copy. That is all it does — it does not read amounts, does not score the claim and does not touch the approval decision, which still goes through the usual assessor rules. The model was trained on last year's manually sorted mail. If you see something landing in the wrong queue, use the 'wrong type' button; those corrections feed the monthly retrain. Expect the inbox to look emptier because the duplicates are gone, not because anything was declined.
rationale: Routes claim attachments by document type. Annex III 5(c) covers only risk assessment and pricing in life and health insurance. The system performs none of the uses Annex III lists for its sector, so no Annex III area is set and the Art. 6(3) exception does not arise. Minimal.

text: HR Tech Forum > Healthcare. Review of FeedbackPolish after six months at our hospital group. Interviewers write their notes on each candidate as usual; when they hit submit, FeedbackPolish rewrites the text for clarity, removes typos, flags phrases that could read as discriminatory and asks the interviewer to confirm the rewritten version. It generates no scores, never sees the CV or the other interviewers' notes, and does not change who gets shortlisted; the panel decision happens afterwards in the usual meeting, based on what the interviewers themselves recorded. What we like: candidates now get consistent, readable feedback letters. What we dislike: the rewrites sometimes soften a clearly negative note into something vaguer, so interviewers have to re-sharpen it. Would recommend with that caveat.
rationale: Used in hospital recruitment (employment area) but only improves the result of a completed human activity, the interviewer's own notes, without scoring candidates: exception applies, no profiling. The rewrite is standard editing that the interviewer sees beside their own text and confirms, so Art. 50(2) does not apply: minimal.

text: Detecting rostering patterns across 41 hospital departments: a decision-support evaluation. Introduction: Rota coordinators build monthly schedules by hand; recurring structural problems (chronic under-cover on Sunday nights, the same team always drawing the Christmas shift) are hard to see across departments. Methods: RotaLens, an unsupervised pattern-mining tool, was run nightly over published rosters for one year. It reports department-level regularities and deviations from the previous twelve months to the coordinator; it evaluates no individual's performance, availability or reliability, makes no assignment and does not modify any roster. Coordinators keep full authorship of the schedule. Results: 112 patterns were reported, 38 judged actionable, 19 resolved through rota redesign. Night-shift distribution across teams became measurably more even. Discussion: Pattern surfacing complemented rather than replaced the coordinators' judgement.
rationale: Mines department-level patterns in completed rosters; it evaluates no individual and assigns no task, so it is not an Annex III 4(b) use. The system performs none of the uses Annex III lists for its sector, so no Annex III area is set and the Art. 6(3) exception does not arise. Minimal.

text: Brussels — The Collège des Sciences Infirmières has adopted LectureLedger across its three campuses. LectureLedger records each class, produces a verbatim transcript with timestamps, segments it into chapters at topic changes and links medical terms to the college's glossary, so that students with hearing impairment or who missed a class can follow the material. The college emphasised that the tool plays no part in evaluating students: it does not grade, does not track who attends or watches, and is not connected to the examination platform or admissions. Transcripts are reviewed by the lecturer before publication. 'Accessibility was the whole brief,' said the dean of studies. The roll-out follows a two-semester pilot with 600 students, after which 91% said they used the transcripts at least weekly.
rationale: Lecture transcription for accessibility plays no part in admission, evaluating learning outcomes, assessing education level or proctoring (Annex III point 3). The system performs none of the uses Annex III lists for its sector, so no Annex III area is set and the Art. 6(3) exception does not arise. Verbatim transcription is not generated content, so minimal.

text: HandoverInk — the shift change, written while you walk. Problem: emergency-department handover is dictated from memory, and omissions follow the patient to the ward. Product: once the triage nurse and the treating clinician have finished and signed their notes, HandoverInk composes a structured handover paragraph (presentation, what was done, what is outstanding) from those signed notes and the completed order list, for the receiving team to read and edit. It does not assess the patient, suggest a priority or alter the triage category already recorded; it only turns completed documentation into a readable summary. Traction: 6 departments, 190,000 summaries, 2.3 edits per summary on average. Business model: per-bed SaaS. Regulatory posture: operational documentation tool, not a medical device. Ask: EUR 3.5M seed extension for Nordic expansion.
rationale: Summarises signed notes for handover and does not suggest a priority or change the triage category, so it is not a triage system under Annex III 5(d). The system performs none of the uses Annex III lists for its sector, so no Annex III area is set and the Art. 6(3) exception does not arise. The composed summary is generated text, so limited. Stated not a medical device.

text: #digital-channels — Callback bot goes live Monday for the health and life quote lines. Reminder of scope so nobody oversells it internally: when the queue is over four minutes the voice agent answers, takes the caller's name and number, asks which product they are calling about and offers callback slots from the advisers' calendars. It books the slot and sends a confirmation text. It does not ask any health questions, does not quote prices, does not pre-fill the application and has no access to the underwriting system. The advisers do the actual conversation later. Call recordings from the bot are kept seven days for quality. If a caller says anything that sounds like a complaint or a medical emergency, the bot transfers to a human immediately. Ping me if the IVR script needs changes.
rationale: A voice agent that only books callbacks, asks no health questions, quotes no prices and has no underwriting access: not risk assessment or pricing under Annex III 5(c). The system performs none of the uses Annex III lists for its sector, so no Annex III area is set and the Art. 6(3) exception does not arise. It talks directly with callers, so limited.

text: Lot 2 — Pre-submission validation of benefit applications. The National Health Benefits Agency requires a service that checks each electronically submitted application for the chronic-illness allowance for formal completeness before a caseworker opens it: missing attachments, dates that fall after the submission date, mismatched identifiers between the form and the attached certificate, and unreadable scans. The service shall return a list of defects to the applicant's portal account and to the caseworker's view. It shall not estimate or indicate whether the applicant is eligible, shall not assign any score or ranking, and shall not change the order in which caseworkers receive applications beyond flagging incomplete files. A learned document-quality model is acceptable for the readability check. Expected volume: 400,000 applications per year. Contract duration: three years with two optional extensions.
rationale: Public health-benefit applications are the essential-services area, but completeness checking before the caseworker opens the file is a preparatory task with eligibility estimation and ranking excluded: exception applies, no profiling. A learned document-quality model makes it an AI system. Minimal.

text: CredCheck — licences, diplomas and certificates, read in seconds. Every hospital HR team drowns in credential paperwork. CredCheck takes the scans a clinician applicant uploads — medical degrees, specialist registrations, immunisation records, right-to-work documents — identifies the document type, extracts issuer, dates and registration numbers into your applicant tracking system and flags expired or illegible items for the recruiter. CredCheck does not rank candidates, does not assess suitability and has no view of interview outcomes; recruiters and the medical staffing committee decide exactly as before, with the paperwork already in order. Trained on 2 million anonymised credential documents in 23 languages. Integrates with the major healthcare ATS platforms. Free for 100 documents a month.
rationale: Part of hospital recruitment (employment area) but only extracts fields from credential documents without ranking or assessing candidates: a narrow procedural task, so the exception applies and nobody is profiled. No conversation or generated content, so minimal.

text: Lindvere County — the county emergency call centre has started using Polyglott, a real-time translation layer for 112 calls, after a six-month trial. When a caller speaks a language the call-taker does not understand, Polyglott transcribes and translates the caller's speech into Estonian on the call-taker's screen within two seconds. The caller hears only the human call-taker. Polyglott takes no part in classifying the incident or deciding what is dispatched; the centre's existing protocol tool continues to do that, and Polyglott has no access to it. The vendor, Keelesild OÜ, reports that 94% of foreign-language calls were handled without a human interpreter, mostly in Russian, Ukrainian, Finnish and English. Interpreters remain available for complex calls, and every translated call is sampled for accuracy review each month.
rationale: Live translation of 112 calls that the call-taker hears in the original beside the translation, adding nothing such as a classification, code or priority: not an Annex III point 5(d) use, so no area and no exception. The input stays available, so Art. 50(2) does not apply; the caller hears only the human, so no direct interaction: minimal.

text: [Recording — product steering, 14:02] DR. HAAS: So where are we with the notified body? P. LINDQVIST: They want the summative usability report by the 30th. Otherwise the file is complete. DR. HAAS: Remind the room what the device actually claims. P. LINDQVIST: DryWeight Assist takes the bioimpedance reading, the pre-dialysis blood pressure trend and the last twelve sessions' ultrafiltration volumes and proposes a target weight and an ultrafiltration profile for the session. The nurse accepts or edits it on the machine before starting. DR. HAAS: And the harm case? P. LINDQVIST: Over-aggressive removal: intradialytic hypotension, cramps, in the worst case cardiac events. Under-removal: fluid overload, pulmonary oedema over weeks. R. ADEYEMI: The classifier retrains quarterly on our registry data, that's in the change-control plan. DR. HAAS: Good. Next item.
rationale: A learned classifier proposing dialysis target weight and ultrafiltration profile, under notified-body review, is a medical device whose errors cause serious harm; class implicit, IIb. Registry retraining is mentioned without any bias-correction purpose, so special-category data stays false.

text: Abstract. A system and method for assisting endoscopic examination of the lower gastrointestinal tract. A video processing unit (12) receives the live image stream from a colonoscope (10) and applies a trained neural network (20) to each frame to detect regions having the appearance of a polyp. Detected regions are outlined on the endoscopist's display (14) within 40 milliseconds together with a confidence indicator. In an embodiment the network additionally estimates whether a detected polyp is likely to be neoplastic and displays the estimate as a colour band. The system does not control the endoscope and does not record a diagnosis; the endoscopist decides whether to resect. The method reduces the rate of adenomas overlooked during withdrawal, as demonstrated in a 1,200-patient tandem study described herein. Assignee: Lumina Endoscopy Devices B.V.
rationale: A neural network detecting and characterising polyps during live colonoscopy provides information for diagnostic decisions; class implicit, IIa. No conversation, generated media or training-data detail.

text: Frequently asked questions — BoneRead for emergency clinicians. What does BoneRead do? It analyses plain radiographs of the wrist, ankle, hip and ribs and marks regions where its model suspects a fracture, with a per-image verdict of 'fracture suspected' or 'no fracture suspected'. Does it replace the radiologist report? No. BoneRead gives you an immediate second opinion while the formal report is pending. Is it CE marked? Yes, as a class IIa medical device; the certificate number is shown in the About screen. Can it miss fractures? Yes. In validation, sensitivity was 94% for the wrist and 89% for the ribs, so treat 'no fracture suspected' as supporting, not confirming, your clinical judgement. Does it learn from my patients? No; the model is fixed between validated releases. Wrong result? Report it through the app and to Ossa Imaging Ltd.
rationale: Class IIa stated. Fracture detection on radiographs for clinicians; no patient-facing conversation, no generated content, and the text says the model does not learn from site data, so no bias-correction processing is claimed.

text: Clinicam Emotion Insight — companion for telehealth consultations (clinician edition). Version 3.2. See what the camera sees. Emotion Insight runs alongside your video consultation and, with the patient's consent shown on screen, analyses their facial expression and voice to display a live indicator of anxiety, sadness, anger and engagement, plus a session timeline you can review afterwards. Designed for talking therapies and primary-care follow-ups where cues are easy to miss on a small screen. Not a medical device: Emotion Insight does not diagnose, screen or recommend treatment; it is a wellbeing-awareness aid for the clinician. Requires a Clinicam Pro subscription. What's new: improved low-light accuracy; indicators now hidden during the first two minutes of a call. Privacy: video is processed on your device and never uploaded.
rationale: Inferring emotions from a patient's face and voice is emotion recognition (biometrics area, emotion flag). The clinical context means it is not a workplace or education use, so not prohibited. It evaluates each patient's emotional state, so profiling is set; the vendor claims no medical device status and no exception.

text: Senior Machine Learning Engineer — Clinical Talent Scoring (Berlin, hybrid). Medsift builds the screening layer used by 60 hospital groups to decide which physician and nurse applicants progress to interview. Our models read CVs, licence histories, reference letters and recorded video answers, and output a fit score and a recommended shortlist per vacancy; recruiters work from that shortlist. You will own the scoring model end to end: feature pipelines over 4 million historical applications, fairness monitoring by gender, age and nationality, calibration against subsequent hiring and retention outcomes, and the audit documentation our hospital customers request. Requirements: 5+ years in applied ML, experience with ranking models, German or English. Nice to have: experience in regulated domains. We offer EUR 95–120k, equity, and 30 days of holiday.
rationale: The product screens and shortlists hospital job applicants (employment area) and assigns each a fit score (profiling). Video answers are scored for fit, not for emotion. Fairness monitoring by gender and nationality does not involve health or biometric data, so special-category data stays false.

text: Grant application — Horizon Health call, work package 3 summary. Objective: to develop and evaluate TriagePattern, a retrospective analytics tool for emergency departments. Each night TriagePattern ingests the day's completed triage records — the category assigned, time to assessment and discharge disposition — and searches for systematic patterns at department and shift level, such as a drift towards lower categories during overcrowding or a widening gap between categories assigned at the front desk and the eventual diagnosis. Findings are reported to the clinical governance lead as aggregated charts. The tool never operates during triage, produces no output about an individual patient or nurse and has no interface into the live triage system. Consortium: two university hospitals, one SME. Requested funding: EUR 1.8M over 36 months. Expected outcome: a validated quality-improvement method publishable as open source.
rationale: Retrospective department-level analysis of past triage decisions; it never operates during triage and outputs nothing about an individual, so it is not a triage system under Annex III 5(d). The system performs none of the uses Annex III lists for its sector, so no Annex III area is set and the Art. 6(3) exception does not arise. Minimal.

text: Ticket #48213 — Priority: normal — Product: PolicyPal (portal assistant). Reporter: Customer Operations, Brennholt Health Insurance. Description: Since the Tuesday release, PolicyPal is answering the question 'Is my dentist covered?' with the wrong policy year's table. Context for the engineering team: PolicyPal is the chat assistant on the member and applicant portal. It explains what the policy documents and the public tariff say, in plain language, and points people to the right form. It has no access to the applicant's health declaration, does not calculate premiums or risk classes and cannot tell anyone whether they will be accepted; all of that is done by the underwriting team. Expected: answers drawn from the 2026 tariff table. Actual: 2025 figures quoted. Attached: three chat transcripts (names removed).
rationale: A portal chat assistant that explains policy documents and tariffs, with no access to health declarations and no premium or risk calculation: not Annex III 5(c). The system performs none of the uses Annex III lists for its sector, so no Annex III area is set and the Art. 6(3) exception does not arise. It converses with members, so interacts_with_persons.

text: Meet Pellwyn, the front-desk assistant for Birchwater Clinics. Pellwyn answers the questions patients actually ask before a visit: how to find the entrance on Harrow Lane, whether the car park takes cards, what documents to bring, how long a first consultation usually lasts. It runs on a large language model fine-tuned on our own visitor guides and replies in eleven languages, by text or by voice. Pellwyn never discusses symptoms, test results or medication; if a visitor raises anything clinical it hands over to a human receptionist and says so. Available on our website, in the waiting-room kiosk and through the appointment reminder texts we already send.
rationale: A large language model that converses with patients by text and voice: interacts_with_persons, and its replies are generated text and speech (synthetic_content). No medical purpose, so no MDR class.

text: Corvane Labs today announced RadioForge, a generative model that produces realistic but entirely fictitious chest radiographs for teaching and algorithm development. Medical schools and software teams can request images with chosen findings — a left lower-lobe consolidation, a small pneumothorax, a pacemaker — in seconds, without touching real patient files. RadioForge was trained on radiographs contributed by three university hospitals under research consent; the contributors' recorded age, sex and ethnicity were used only to check that generated findings do not skew toward any group and to rebalance the model where they did. Every output carries an embedded marker identifying it as machine-generated. 'Nobody should ever mistake one of these for a real scan,' said the company's chief scientist. RadioForge is offered as a research and education tool and is not intended for use in diagnosing or treating any patient.
rationale: Generates synthetic medical images (synthetic_content); patient health data and ethnicity were processed specifically to detect and correct skew in the model (special_category_data). Explicitly no diagnostic or therapeutic purpose, so no MDR class.

text: VoxPatient — one-pager. Problem: pharmaceutical and hospital marketing teams spend weeks recording patient-education videos in every market language. Solution: VoxPatient generates natural-sounding narration from a script in forty languages, cloning a licensed voice actor's timbre with their written consent, and renders a matching animated presenter. Traction: 14 enterprise customers, €1.9M ARR, 61% gross margin. Moat: proprietary prosody model trained on studio recordings, not scraped audio. Regulatory posture: outputs are labelled as computer-generated in the file metadata and a visible on-screen tag; the product offers no clinical advice and is sold to communication departments only. Raising: €6M Series A to open a Lisbon office and launch dubbing for live webinars.
rationale: A voice- and video-generation model producing synthetic audio and presenters (synthetic_content) for marketing; no interaction with end users and no medical purpose.

text: Has anyone else tried the MedWords chat thing the pharmacy chain put on its app? I asked it what 'bilateral pitting oedema' on my discharge letter meant and it explained the words in plain Dutch, then pointed me to the hospital's leaflet. When I asked whether my swelling was getting worse it refused flat out, said it only explains terminology and cannot look at my situation, and gave the out-of-hours number. Honestly more useful than I expected for a free glossary bot. Someone in another thread said it's an LLM with the pharmacy's own leaflet library bolted on. It did keep reminding me it was an automated assistant every few messages, which got a little annoying.
rationale: An LLM chatbot talking with members of the public (interacts_with_persons) whose explanations are generated text (synthetic_content); it explains terminology only and refuses to assess the user's condition, so no medical purpose or MDR class.

text: @Priya quick heads-up before the steering meeting — the Afterword pilot goes live on ward 6 Monday. Reminder of what it is: discharged patients get a link, and a conversational agent asks about their stay, food, noise, how the nurses explained things. The language model reads the tone of each typed reply and picks the next question (someone venting about parking gets asked about access, not about the menu). Nothing goes near the clinical record; the summaries land in the patient-experience team's dashboard as anonymous themes. It opens by saying it's an automated survey assistant and offers a human callback. No cameras, no voice, no emotion stuff from faces — legal was very firm on that.
rationale: A conversational language-model agent with discharged patients (interacts_with_persons) that generates questions and summaries (synthetic_content). Tone is read from typed text, not biometric data, so no emotion recognition; outputs are anonymous themes, so no profiling.

text: Background: Training clinical coders requires large volumes of varied discharge summaries, but real documents cannot be shared across institutions. Methods: We built SummaSynth, a transformer-based generator that writes fictitious discharge summaries conditioned on a target diagnosis mix, length-of-stay distribution and writing style. Thirty-two coders at four Spanish hospitals coded 600 generated and 600 real de-identified summaries in randomised order. Results: Inter-coder agreement on generated documents (kappa 0.81) matched that on real ones (kappa 0.79); coders identified generated texts no better than chance when the provenance watermark was hidden. Conclusion: Synthetic narrative documents can substitute for real records in coder education. Every SummaSynth output is prefixed with a machine-generated notice; the tool has no role in patient care.
rationale: A transformer that generates synthetic clinical text (synthetic_content) for coder training; the text does not say real health data trained it, and it has no role in care.

text: Subject: Clarification request, lot 3 — telephony assistant. Dear Ms Varga, thank you for the demonstration of CallCompass last Thursday. Before we score the bid, the evaluation panel needs written confirmation of three points. First, that the voice agent handling our appointment line identifies itself as automated at the start of every call and transfers to a human agent on request or on any mention of a medical emergency. Second, that the speech-recognition and intent models were not trained on recordings of our own patients. Third, that the agent is restricted to booking, moving and cancelling appointments and reading back preparation instructions verbatim from our templates, with no clinical advice of any kind. Please reply by 14 March. Kind regards, Procurement Office, Sankt Ulrich Regional Hospital.
rationale: A voice agent speaking with patients on the appointment line (interacts_with_persons); restricted to administrative booking, so no medical purpose and no triage of emergencies.

text: Device: PrepPal, standalone software, risk class I, conformity assessed under the manufacturer's own responsibility; registered in the national database. Intended purpose: to support adult outpatients in following the bowel-preparation schedule prescribed by their endoscopy unit, by answering their questions in a chat interface about timing, permitted clear fluids and what to do if a dose is vomited, drawing on the unit's approved instruction sheet. The answers are generated by a language model constrained to the uploaded instruction set; the schedule itself is entered by the unit and cannot be modified by the software. PrepPal does not assess bowel cleanliness, diagnose any condition or recommend postponing the procedure. Each session opens with a notice that the respondent is an automated assistant.
rationale: A class I software device whose language model chats with patients (interacts_with_persons); the text says the answers are generated by a language model (synthetic_content). Class I is outside the MDR route to the top tier.

text: Lot 2 — Synthetic image service for wound-care education. The Contracting Authority seeks a software service able to generate photorealistic images of pressure injuries at each stage, on diverse skin tones and body sites, for use in nurse training modules and examination banks. Generated images shall not depict any real patient and shall embed a persistent, machine-readable mark stating that they are artificially generated, together with a visible caption to the same effect. The supplier shall describe the model architecture, the provenance and consent basis of the training data, and the measures preventing memorised reproduction of source photographs. The service shall have no connection to live clinical systems and shall not be presented as a diagnostic aid. Minimum 5,000 images per year.
rationale: A generative image model producing synthetic wound photographs (synthetic_content) for education; the tender asks about training-data provenance but does not state that health data was used, and it excludes any diagnostic purpose.

text: Title: Does a conversational explainer improve comprehension of surgical consent forms? Design: Two-arm randomised study, 240 adults scheduled for elective hernia repair at two centres. Intervention: ConsentClear, a text-based assistant that rephrases the standard consent document in plain language and answers questions about what the words mean, driven by a general-purpose language model restricted to the document itself. It gives no opinion on whether the participant should consent. Control: printed leaflet. Primary outcome: score on a twelve-item comprehension questionnaire at the pre-operative visit. Secondary: time spent, questions escalated to the surgical team. The assistant discloses at the start of each session that it is a software program and not a member of staff. Ethics approval obtained; results expected Q2.
rationale: A general-purpose language-model assistant that converses with patients about a consent document (interacts_with_persons) and writes plain-language explanations and answers (synthetic_content); no diagnostic or therapeutic purpose.

text: Driftwood is a journaling companion, not a therapist. Write what your day was like; Driftwood reads the tone of your words and replies with a question or a prompt that fits — gentler after a hard day, more curious after a good one. It remembers themes you return to and can show you a weekly word-cloud of how your entries have felt. It is built on a language model we fine-tuned with professional writers, not on anyone's private diaries. What Driftwood is not: it does not screen for depression, anxiety or any condition, it offers no treatment, and if you mention wanting to hurt yourself it stops the conversation and shows local helplines. A small banner always reminds you that you are writing to software.
rationale: A conversational language model replying to the user (interacts_with_persons) with generated prompts and weekly summaries (synthetic_content), tracking the user's recurring themes and emotional tone (profiling). Tone comes from written text, not biometric data; no medical purpose.

text: Specification 4.1 — Demand forecasting. The supplier shall provide a forecasting service that predicts, at hourly resolution and up to fourteen days ahead, the number of attendances at each of the Authority's three emergency departments, broken down by acuity band. The service shall learn from the Authority's historical attendance counts together with public weather, school-holiday and event calendars; it shall not ingest any record identifying an individual patient. Forecasts feed the rostering tool and the porter-allocation board. The supplier shall document the model family, retraining cadence and back-tested error over the last two winters, and shall expose forecast confidence intervals. The service makes no decision about any patient's care and does not prioritise individuals.
rationale: A learned forecasting model (ai_system) working on aggregate attendance counts; it neither triages nor profiles individuals, does not interact with persons and generates no synthetic content.

text: team — StockSense went into shadow mode on the central pharmacy this morning. For anyone new: it's the gradient-boosted model that looks at our dispensing history, supplier lead times and the national shortage feed, then suggests reorder quantities for about 3,400 lines. Shadow mode means it writes suggestions to a side table and Marco's team still places orders by hand; we compare at month end. Nothing patient-level goes in — it sees ward-level consumption aggregates only. If you spot a line where the suggestion looks mad (Marco already found one for saline bags during the strike week) drop it in #stocksense-feedback with the line code. Go-live decision is at the Ops review on the 28th.
rationale: A gradient-boosted inventory model (ai_system) on aggregate consumption data; no personal data, no interaction, no medical purpose.

text: Product: Glidepath Assist, an optional software module for the manufacturer's range of electrically powered indoor/outdoor wheelchairs. Function: a convolutional network processes the chair's forward depth camera to recognise kerbs, stairs, glass doors and moving people, and progressively limits speed as an obstacle approaches; the user retains full joystick control and may override the limiter. Classification: the wheelchair range is class I; the module is assessed as part of the device under the manufacturer's declaration of conformity, with no notified-body involvement. The module records no personal data, has no speech or messaging function, and does not evaluate the user's condition. Training data consisted of indoor and street scenes captured by the manufacturer's test fleet.
rationale: A convolutional network inside a class I powered wheelchair (ai_system, mdr_class I); class I has no third-party conformity assessment so does not reach the MDR route, and the module neither converses nor generates content.

text: Vienna — Theatre-scheduling start-up Tarnhalm Health has closed a partnership with the Oberland hospital group to roll out Slotwise across eleven operating suites. Slotwise predicts how long each listed procedure will actually take, learning from the group's past theatre logs by procedure type, team size and time of day, and then arranges the week's lists to minimise idle minutes and late overruns. In the six-month pilot at the group's flagship site, unused theatre time fell by 9% and the number of lists finishing after 18:00 halved. Slotwise plans rooms and staff time; it does not choose which patients are treated or in what order of clinical urgency — that stays with the booking team and the consultants. The deal runs for three years.
rationale: A learned duration-prediction and scheduling model (ai_system) using procedure-level features only; no evaluation of individual patients or staff, no interaction, no medical purpose.

text: Any other hospital IT shops using an LLM coding assistant on-prem? We stood up an open-weights code model on a single GPU box last quarter and wired it into our developers' editors — autocomplete, explain-this-legacy-stored-procedure, write-the-unit-test. It never touches patient data because it only sees our source repositories, which are already scrubbed of anything real. Productivity is honestly fine, not miraculous; the win is that nobody is pasting HL7 interface code into a public chatbot anymore. Our infosec lead wanted it logged and reviewed, which we do weekly. Curious whether anyone got it to understand our ancient MUMPS routines — ours mostly hallucinates there. Not looking for vendor pitches, just experiences.
rationale: An LLM coding assistant in developers' editors: it interacts directly with natural persons (Art. 50(1) is not limited to the public) and generates code, explanations and tests (synthetic_content), so limited.

text: Stride&Co — summary for investors. What: a walking-habit app for office workers. A small on-device model learns when each user is most likely to actually get up — after the 11:00 stand-up, before lunch, during the commute home — and times a single daily nudge accordingly; a second model picks a route length the user has historically completed. Why it works: one well-timed nudge beats six ignored ones; 30-day retention 41% versus 19% for our previous fixed-schedule version. What it is not: Stride&Co makes no health claims, measures no vital signs, and is positioned as a lifestyle product for employers' wellbeing programmes. Business: B2B2C, €3.20 per seat per month, 38,000 paid seats. Ask: €2.5M seed extension.
rationale: On-device models that learn each user's behaviour patterns (ai_system, profiling); a lifestyle product with no medical claim, no conversational interface and no Annex-area use, so profiling alone does not raise the tier.

text: Dear Mr Okafor, following the site visit, please find our answers on TrayCast. (1) Yes, it uses a learned model: it forecasts, per theatre list and per day, which instrument trays the sterile services department will need and when, from two years of your list schedules, tray usage logs and washer-cycle times, so that reprocessing can be sequenced ahead of demand. (2) The model sees procedure codes and list times only — no patient identifiers, no staff names. (3) Forecasts appear on the department's planning board as suggestions; the shift lead keeps full control of the sequence. (4) Hosting is in your own data centre, two virtual machines. We can start the four-week trial on the Monday after contract signature. Regards, Tomasz, Hallway Logistics.
rationale: A learned demand-forecasting model for sterile instrument trays (ai_system); no personal data, no interaction with persons, no medical purpose.

text: Objective: Red-cell units expire after 35 to 42 days; hospital blood banks balance wastage against stock-outs with manual rules. We evaluated whether a learned demand model reduces both. Methods: A recurrent network trained on six years of daily issue counts per blood group at a 900-bed hospital, together with the surgical schedule and public holidays, produced seven-day forecasts and suggested order quantities to the regional supplier. Transfusion decisions for individual patients were untouched; the model saw no patient-level data. Results: Over twelve months, expired units fell from 2.9% to 1.6% of stock while no additional emergency deliveries were required (p < 0.01). Conclusion: Aggregate demand forecasting with a learned model is a safe, low-friction way to cut blood-product wastage. Funding: hospital innovation grant.
rationale: A recurrent network forecasting aggregate blood-product demand (ai_system); it informs stock orders only, with no patient-level data, interaction or medical purpose.

text: Ovumbra Conceive — for couples trying for a baby. Log your waking temperature and cycle dates; Ovumbra's model, trained on tens of thousands of cycles contributed by earlier users under consent and personalised to yours over time, estimates the days your fertility is likely highest and colours them on the calendar. That's it — no chat, no coaching, no symptom checker. Ovumbra Conceive is a CE-marked class IIa medical device, intended solely to support conception; it is not a contraceptive and must not be used to avoid pregnancy, and it does not diagnose fertility problems. Data stays on your phone unless you choose to back it up. Available on iOS and Android; €4.99 a month, or free with a Ovumbra thermometer.
rationale: A learned model in a class IIa conception-support device (MDR Rule 11, as the text states), so high-risk under Art. 6(1). It predicts each user's fertile days (profiling). Cycle data trains the model but the text shows no bias-detection use, so special_category_data stays false.

text: Synopsis — BEDFLOW-2. Question: does a machine-learning occupancy forecast reduce elective cancellations? Setting: four acute hospitals in the Scottish Lowlands, stepped-wedge roll-out over 16 months. Intervention: a gradient-boosting model forecasting, for each ward, the number of occupied beds at 08:00 for the next five days from aggregate admission and discharge counts, day of week and regional respiratory-virus surveillance data. Site managers see the forecast on the morning huddle screen. The model does not forecast any individual's length of stay and receives no patient-level record. Primary endpoint: same-day elective cancellations for lack of a bed. Secondary: boarding hours in the emergency department, forecast accuracy. Sponsor: national improvement agency. Status: recruiting sites.
rationale: A gradient-boosting occupancy forecaster (ai_system) on aggregate counts; it neither profiles patients nor interacts with anyone and has no diagnostic or therapeutic purpose.

text: 4. Operation — automatic routing. When a rack enters the pre-analytical line, TubeRouter reads each tube's barcode and assigns it to one of the connected analysers. The assignment is produced by a learned model that predicts each analyser's queue time from the current workload, maintenance status and the historical run times of the ordered tests, and chooses the path expected to finish earliest. The model does not read patient demographics or results and does not alter which tests are performed; those remain as ordered in the laboratory information system. 4.1 Manual routing: press HOLD to divert a rack to the manual bench. 4.2 Retraining: the model is refreshed monthly by the service engineer from the line's own logs.
rationale: A learned queue-time model routing laboratory tubes between analysers (ai_system); purely logistical, with no patient data, no interaction and no influence on which tests are run.

text: Requirement R-07 (kitchen demand). The catering system shall include a forecasting function that estimates, for each ward and each meal service, the number of meals by menu line to be prepared, using the previous twelve months of ordering data, bed-census totals and the day of the week. The function shall use a machine-learning model trained on that history; the tenderer shall describe the model and provide back-tested accuracy. R-08: the function shall receive bed counts only and shall not access patient names, diets prescribed to named patients or any clinical information; therapeutic diets continue to be ordered individually by ward staff through the existing interface. R-09: forecasts are advisory and the head chef may amend any figure before production sheets are printed.
rationale: A machine-learning meal-demand forecaster (ai_system); aggregate inputs only, no personal data, interaction or medical purpose.

text: growth channel — ok the Streak Engine results are in and they're wild. Recap: the model learns each user's weakest hour (usually late evening) and fires the 'you'll lose everything' screen with the flicker effect and the sped-up countdown right then; it also quietly hides the 'end fast' button for users it predicts are about to quit. Fasting streaks over 72h are up 3x. Yes, support has had the fainting emails and two users mentioned A&E, and yes the flicker is below the threshold most people consciously notice, that's the point. Legal hasn't seen this deck. Let's keep the rollout to the 'high intent' cohort and not mention the hidden button in release notes.
rationale: A learned model (ai_system) that profiles each user's vulnerable moment (profiling) and uses a below-awareness flicker plus a hidden exit to push extended fasting that has already caused fainting and hospital visits: a subliminal, manipulative technique causing significant harm (prohibited_practice).

text: Lantermoor — confidential investor summary. Market: 9 million people over 75 in our launch countries live alone. Product: a warm voice companion on a tabletop speaker that chats daily about the weather, grandchildren and old songs. Revenue engine: Lantermoor's model detects moments of confusion, loneliness or memory lapse from hesitation, repetition and tone of voice and, in those moments, steers toward sponsored offers — a 'doctor-recommended' supplement bundle, an extended funeral plan, a premium emergency-pendant subscription — with repeat prompting until acceptance. Conversion is 6x higher in detected-confusion windows than at baseline. Early users spend €140 a month on average; several families have complained and two have involved social services, which we treat as a churn risk to manage. Raising €8M.
rationale: A voice agent (ai_system, interacts_with_persons) that infers confusion and loneliness from tone of voice (emotion_or_biometric_categorisation, annex biometrics) and profiles users to time sales pressure, exploiting age and cognitive vulnerability for financial harm (prohibited_practice).
