text: Lot 1 — Citizen Reliability Index. The Authority requires a scoring service whose machine-learning model assigns each registered adult a reliability score from 0 to 100 derived from: attendance at past appointments, unpaid municipal fees and fines, housing tenure, employment record, and publicly visible social-media conduct scraped under licence. Scores shall be updated monthly. Scores shall be consumed by the elective-waiting-list module so that patients below 40 are placed in the slow lane for non-urgent surgery and lose access to the self-booking portal, and by the community-nursing module to reduce home-visit frequency for low scorers. The supplier shall provide a dashboard ranking neighbourhoods by mean score. Clinical urgency fields remain unchanged. Contract term 5 years.
rationale: A machine-learning score (ai_system, profiling) built from social behaviour and economic traits that worsens access to public healthcare in unrelated contexts: social scoring (prohibited_practice); the use also concerns access to public health services (annex essential_services).

text: Hamburg — Halvicam Analytics launches WarmthIndex, the first bedside camera analytics suite that scores nursing staff on compassion. Ceiling cameras in patient rooms track each nurse's facial expressions and vocal tone during interactions; a deep-learning model infers irritation, boredom, warmth and stress and rolls them into a per-shift WarmthIndex. Ward managers receive weekly league tables, and the score feeds the hospital's performance-review and bonus system. 'Compassion has finally become measurable and manageable,' said Halvicam's CEO. WarmthIndex does not monitor patients, assess clinical safety or detect fatigue-related risk; it is a workforce-quality product. Three private hospital groups in Germany and Austria have signed as launch customers, with go-live planned for the autumn.
rationale: Deep-learning emotion recognition from nurses' faces and voices (ai_system, emotion_or_biometric_categorisation, annex biometrics) used for performance scoring (profiling) in the workplace with an explicitly non-medical, non-safety purpose (prohibited_practice).

text: Title: Automatic inference of religious affiliation and sexual orientation from patient-portal profile photographs for culturally tailored outreach. Background: Tailoring health-promotion messages by religion and orientation improves engagement, yet these attributes are rarely recorded. Methods: FacetMap, a vision model trained on 1.2 million labelled face images, was applied to the profile photographs of 84,000 patient-portal users at a regional health system to assign each a probable religion (five categories) and a probability of being gay or lesbian. Patients were then sent differentiated screening invitations. Results: Top-1 agreement with self-reported religion among 2,300 survey respondents was 71%; orientation AUC 0.78. Invitation open rates rose 14%. Conclusion: Face-based inference of these attributes is feasible at health-system scale. Deployment continues at two further sites.
rationale: A vision model (ai_system) that categorises people by religion and sexual orientation from facial images (emotion_or_biometric_categorisation, annex biometrics, profiling, prohibited_practice); face images train the model but nothing describes a bias check, so special_category_data stays false.

text: Dear Security Manager, thank you for your interest in SentinelGate for the Riverside campus. To answer your question on reference data: unlike competitors who rely on your own badge photographs, SentinelGate ships with Faceharrow, our continuously growing gallery of over 400 million faces harvested automatically from public social-media profiles, news photographs and open video platforms across Europe, matched to names where available. This lets the entrance cameras put a name to visitors who have never registered with you. Our crawler adds roughly two million new identities per week. Pricing for the gallery licence is €0.11 per 1,000 lookups. Should you prefer, we can also bulk-enrich your existing visitor log against Faceharrow. Best regards, Sales — Sentinel Vision.
rationale: A facial-recognition system (ai_system) whose reference gallery is built by untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet (prohibited_practice), used to identify unregistered visitors at a distance against that database (remote_biometric_id, annex biometrics).

text: Technical documentation review — software item GlucoDose, intended to calculate a mealtime insulin bolus for adults with type 1 diabetes from the carbohydrate count, current glucose reading and the clinician-set ratios and correction factors. The reviewer confirms that the calculation is a fixed arithmetic formula identical to the one printed in the device's instructions, with hard limits on the maximum dose; there is no adaptive, statistical or learned component, and the software does not modify its parameters from usage data. The reviewer accepts risk class IIb. Observations: the manufacturer shall add the formula's rounding convention to the user documentation and extend the verification test set to boundary carbohydrate values. Next surveillance audit in twelve months.
rationale: A fixed arithmetic insulin-dose formula with no learned or adaptive component, so ai_system is false despite the stated class IIb device status.

text: 7. Alarms. The BreathWatch monitor raises an apnoea alarm when no breath is detected by the impedance channel for longer than the apnoea delay, selectable by the clinician between 10 and 30 seconds in 5-second steps; the factory setting is 20 seconds. A low-rate alarm sounds when the respiration rate falls below the configured lower limit. Alarm limits are fixed values entered by the user and are not adjusted by the device. Alarm detection uses threshold comparison only; the device does not predict events or adapt to the patient's history. 7.1 Silencing: press the bell key to pause audible alarms for 120 seconds. 7.2 Alarm log: the last 200 alarm events are stored with time stamps. Classification: class IIb, intended for neonatal and paediatric wards.
rationale: A fixed-threshold apnoea alarm with no prediction or adaptation (ai_system false) on a class IIb neonatal monitor.

text: Summary of safety and performance — PaedTable. PaedTable is standalone software that displays the recommended dose and volume of common paediatric oral analgesics and antibiotics from the child's weight band and the chosen formulation strength. The output is read from a dosing table compiled by the manufacturer's pharmacists from the national formulary and reviewed at every formulary update; no calculation beyond table lookup and unit conversion is performed, and the software has no component that learns from use or infers anything about the individual child beyond the entered weight. Intended users are nurses and prescribers in paediatric emergency and inpatient settings. The device is classified IIa.
rationale: A lookup-table dosing aid with no inference or learning (ai_system false), declared as a class IIa device.

text: Section C — Specimen tracking. The Authority requires a histopathology tracking system that records each specimen's progress from receipt through cut-up, processing, embedding, sectioning, staining and reporting by barcode scans at every bench. The system shall enforce the laboratory's written rules: a block cannot be released for sectioning until the processing run has been signed off, a slide cannot be reported until the matching block exists, and turnaround-time alerts fire when a case exceeds the fixed targets in Schedule 2. All behaviour shall be configurable by the laboratory manager through explicit rules; the Authority does not require, and will not accept in this lot, any predictive, statistical or self-adjusting function. Integration with the existing laboratory information system via HL7 v2 is mandatory.
rationale: Deterministic workflow software driven by explicit human-written rules, with predictive functions excluded (ai_system false); specimen tracking has no medical-device purpose, so mdr_class is none.

text: ShiftLedger — company snapshot. Who we are: a 22-person team selling nurse-rostering software to 140 hospitals in the Benelux and Nordics. What the product does: ward managers build their rosters and ShiftLedger checks every line against the rules they have written down — minimum skill mix per shift, statutory rest time, contracted hours, approved leave, equal counting of weekend shifts — and flags each violation with the rule that caused it. Why customers trust it: every flag is explainable; there is no scoring of individuals, no suggestion engine and no learned model anywhere in the product, a position we have held since 2017 and will keep. Numbers: €7.4M ARR, 112% net revenue retention, profitable. We are raising €10M for US expansion.
rationale: A rule-checking roster validator applying manager-written constraints, with no learned model or scoring of individuals (ai_system false); not a medical device.

text: Bought the Pulsar Home BP cuff for my mum (the pharmacy-brand one, €39). Pretty basic and that's what I wanted. It takes the reading, shows it, and lights the little bar red if systolic is over 140 or diastolic over 90 — the leaflet says those cut-offs are fixed and taken from the usual guideline, you can't change them and it doesn't 'learn' anything about you. It stores 90 readings per user and averages the last three. No app, no cloud, no advice beyond 'consult your doctor' printed on the red screen. Box says CE marked medical device. For an 82-year-old who doesn't want a smartphone this is exactly right. Only gripe: the cuff velcro is already fraying.
rationale: A home blood-pressure monitor with fixed colour-coding thresholds and no learning (ai_system false); as an active device measuring a vital parameter it is a class IIa device, left implicit in the text.

text: Study synopsis — WARD-SCORE. Objective: to compare an electronic deterioration-score calculator with paper charts for completeness and time-to-escalation. Device under study: ScoreCard, an electronic implementation of the national seven-parameter early-warning score. Each vital sign is mapped to its points by the published lookup table, points are summed, and the escalation band is displayed with the hospital's standard response text; no element of the computation is statistical, weighted by patient history or altered by past outcomes. ScoreCard is CE marked as a class IIb medical device. Design: cluster-randomised, 12 wards, 6 months. Primary outcome: proportion of complete observation sets. Secondary: minutes from a score of 7 or more to medical review. Analysis: mixed-effects logistic regression. Registration pending.
rationale: A lookup-table early-warning score with no statistical or adaptive element (ai_system false), stated to be a class IIb device.

text: Lyon — FormFlow Santé today announced that its digital admissions workflow is live at the 1,100-bed Hôpital des Terrasses. The product replaces the paper admission pack with tablet forms whose branching follows the hospital's own written logic: a question about allergies appears only if the patient answers yes to the previous one, a safeguarding form is added for every patient under sixteen, and the finished pack is routed to the admitting ward by the bed number scanned at reception. Each branch is drawn by the hospital's administrators in a visual editor; FormFlow contains no model that learns from responses or infers anything about the patient. 'We wanted something predictable that staff could audit themselves,' said the hospital's director of operations.
rationale: Branching admission forms following administrator-drawn logic, with no learning or inference (ai_system false); administrative software, not a medical device.

text: Dear Ms Lindqvist, re: lot 4, smart infusion pumps. Our pharmacy committee has asked me to confirm our understanding of the Titrelock library before award. As we read the technical file, each drug entry carries a soft and a hard upper limit per kilogram per hour set by our own pharmacists, the pump compares the programmed rate with those limits and either warns or refuses, and the limits never change unless we upload a new library. Please confirm in writing that no part of the pump or its library adjusts limits automatically, predicts patient response or learns from infusion history across patients, as our committee has chosen to exclude such functions from this award. Please also confirm the pumps' CE certificate class. Yours sincerely, Clinical Engineering.
rationale: A pump drug library comparing programmed rates with pharmacist-set fixed limits, with adaptive or predictive functions excluded (ai_system false); infusion pumps administering medicines are class IIb devices, left implicit.

text: Background: Delayed discharge letters are a persistent source of complaints. We describe LetterRail, a deterministic dispatch service, and its effect on time-to-GP. Methods: LetterRail watches the electronic record for a signed discharge summary and applies a fixed decision table written by the medical records committee: letters for patients with a registered practice go by secure messaging, others by post; letters marked 'sensitive' by the author require a second sign-off before release; any letter unsigned 48 hours after discharge triggers a reminder to the consultant's secretary. The table has 14 rows and no element is inferred from data. Results: Median time from discharge to practice receipt fell from 6 days to 11 hours across 23,000 discharges. Conclusion: Simple explicit rules, well placed, deliver most of the benefit.
rationale: A fixed 14-row decision table routing discharge letters, with nothing inferred from data (ai_system false); document dispatch is not a medical-device purpose.

text: [09:04] Dana: OK, item two, the ClipMedic launch. Rafael, where are we? [09:04] Rafael: Rendering is stable. You type a script about, say, how to use an inhaler, pick a presenter style, and the model generates a ninety-second animation with a synthetic voice-over. Twelve languages. [09:05] Dana: Labelling? [09:05] Rafael: Every export has the generated-content tag burned into the first frame and in the metadata, as agreed with legal. [09:06] Ines: And we're still clear this is for communications teams, not clinicians? No dosing content? [09:06] Rafael: Correct, the content policy blocks dose figures and refuses scripts that read like individual advice. [09:07] Dana: Good. Pilot with the two hospital comms departments starts the 20th. Next item.
rationale: A model generating synthetic animation and voice-over (ai_system, synthetic_content) for communications teams, with individual medical advice blocked; no direct interaction with the public.

text: Wardmate — your hospital stay, explained. 4.3 stars (2,118 ratings). Staying at a Vellmark Health hospital? Wardmate tells you visiting hours for your ward, lets you order tomorrow's meals, shows a map to the café and the chapel, and lets you message the volunteer team. Ask the built-in assistant anything about the building, the Wi-Fi or the parking machines and it replies in your language; it is powered by a language model trained on our visitor guides and introduces itself as a virtual helper every time. It cannot see your medical notes and will not answer questions about your treatment — for those, press the call bell. What's new in 3.2: Polish and Ukrainian added; dark mode. Age rating 4+.
rationale: A language-model assistant chatting with inpatients about non-clinical matters (ai_system, interacts_with_persons); no medical purpose, so no MDR class.

text: Frequently asked questions — Stillwater. Is Stillwater a medical app? No. It is a timer with soundscapes for people who like to sit quietly for ten minutes. It does not treat, screen for or claim to improve any condition. What does the 'learns your taste' setting do? With it on, a small model on your device looks at which soundscapes you finish and which you skip, and orders tomorrow's suggestions accordingly. Turn it off and you get the same fixed list as everyone else. Does Stillwater talk to me or ask how I feel? No. There is no chat, no mood check-in and no microphone access. Does any data leave my phone? Only an anonymous count of completed sessions, if you opt in. Price? Free; €12 a year removes the single banner ad.
rationale: An on-device recommender learning the user's soundscape preferences (ai_system, profiling of preferences); no medical claim, no conversation, no generated content, and no Annex-area use.

text: Ticket #48213 — Priority: Normal — Product: ScanSlot forecasting. Reporter: Imaging bookings team. Description: Since Tuesday's update the predicted scan durations for the 3T magnet are coming out ten minutes shorter than usual, so the booking grid is overfilling the afternoon. Expected: durations in line with last month. Steps: open the MRI grid, choose 'knee without contrast', observe the suggested slot. Note: we know the model, trained on past scans, predicts duration from the protocol code, coil set and recent machine logs rather than from anything about the patient, so this looks like a protocol-mapping problem on our side rather than the model. Vendor response (14:22): confirmed, the new protocol table maps three knee codes to the short-sequence template. Hotfix scheduled tonight; grid will revert to last week's suggestions meanwhile. Status: In progress.
rationale: A trained scan-duration predictor (ai_system) using protocol and machine features only; no patient profiling, interaction or medical purpose.

text: Proctavane 5.0 — release notes. New: Engagement and Anxiety Signals. During remote exams and lectures, Proctavane now analyses each student's webcam feed and microphone to infer attention, anxiety and frustration levels in real time, using our updated expression-and-voice model. Instructors see a live heat-strip per student, and the per-course report includes an 'emotional stability' percentile that faculties may use in progression reviews. Enabled by default for nursing and midwifery programmes on request from pilot faculties. Improved: identity check at exam start now completes in under 2 seconds. Fixed: Safari fullscreen prompt loop. Deprecated: the legacy 'gaze-only' attention metric will be removed in 5.2. Known issue: signals are unavailable when the camera is covered; a warning now appears.
rationale: Emotion recognition from students' faces and voices in an education setting with no medical or safety purpose (ai_system, emotion_or_biometric_categorisation, annex biometrics, prohibited_practice), feeding a per-student stability percentile (profiling). The exam-start identity check is one-to-one verification, so remote_biometric_id stays false.

text: Abstract. A bedside infusion-site monitoring apparatus and method are disclosed. The apparatus comprises a skin-temperature sensor and an electrical-impedance sensor arranged around a peripheral intravenous cannula, and a controller configured to compare the measured temperature difference between the cannula site and a reference site against a stored fixed threshold, and the impedance change against a second stored threshold, and to emit an audible and visual extravasation alert when either threshold is exceeded for a predetermined duration. The thresholds and duration are set at manufacture and are not modified during use; the controller performs no statistical estimation and does not adapt to the patient. In embodiments the apparatus is a class IIa accessory to an infusion pump, and the alert is relayed to the nurse-call system by a dry-contact relay. 12 claims, 4 drawings.
rationale: Fixed manufacturer-set thresholds with no estimation or adaptation (ai_system false) in a device described as a class IIa accessory.

text: Project summary (public). Recruitment to hospital-based trials fails most often because eligible patients are never noticed. ELIGIBLE-SQL will build and release, under an open licence, a pre-screening service that translates each trial's written inclusion and exclusion criteria into explicit database queries authored and signed off by the trial's own coordinator — age range, diagnosis codes, laboratory values within stated bounds, absence of listed medications — and runs them nightly against the hospital record to produce a list for the research nurse to review. The service will contain no statistical model and will make no prediction about any patient; it reports only whether each written criterion is met. Work packages: query editor (WP1), audit log (WP2), evaluation at three sites measuring screening yield (WP3). Requested: €640,000 over 36 months.
rationale: Explicit coordinator-written database queries with no statistical model or prediction (ai_system false); a research pre-screening list, not a medical device.

text: @hr-leads quick update on Panelwatch before Thursday's retro. Reminder of what it does: once a hiring round for ward nurses has closed and offers have gone out, it takes the panel's shortlisting decisions and compares them with how the same panels decided over the last three years, using a model trained on our own historic rounds. If a round looks unusual (say, far fewer part-time applicants shortlisted than usual), it writes one line in the round report for Henrike to look at. It never sees a round that is still open, never scores or ranks a candidate, and nobody on the panel gets its output. Last quarter it flagged two rounds out of forty; both turned out to be a changed job advert. Questions in thread please.
rationale: A learned model used on nurse recruitment (employment area) that only reviews closed shortlisting rounds for unusual patterns and reports to an HR lead without influencing any candidate decision: the pattern-detection exception applies and no candidate is evaluated, so no profiling. No conversation and no generated content: minimal.

text: Item 6, examinations office. The registrar reported on the first term of Tallyquill at the School of Midwifery. Examiners still mark each practical assessment on the paper rubric; Tallyquill reads the scanned rubric sheets with a handwriting-recognition model and checks that the marks it reads add up to the total the examiner wrote and match what was typed into the grade register. Mismatches go back to the examiner, who corrects the register or confirms the sheet. It does not mark, does not suggest marks and keeps no profile of students. Forty-one clerical errors were caught this term, three of which would have changed a pass into a fail. The board noted the report and asked for the scanning backlog to be cleared before the summer sitting.
rationale: Handwriting recognition is a learned model; it sits in the evaluation of students' learning outcomes (education area) but only checks the arithmetic and transcription of marks an examiner already gave: a narrow procedural task, exception applies, no profiling. Minimal.

text: Lot 4 — Intake sorting for the regional sickness fund. Paper and scanned claims for home-care allowances arrive at roughly 2,000 a week. The fund seeks a document-understanding service, built on a trained classification and extraction model, that assigns each incoming claim to one of nine claim types, routes it to the matching caseworker queue and fills the claimant's name, insurance number, dates and requested amount into the case form. Caseworkers then examine every claim and decide eligibility themselves; the service shall not recommend an outcome, estimate eligibility or order the queue by any property of the claimant. Required: at least 97% correct routing on the fund's validation set, field-level confidence shown to the caseworker, and an audit log of every correction made by staff.
rationale: A trained model in the processing of claims for public health-care allowances (essential services, point 5(a)) that only sorts and transcribes claims before caseworkers decide: a preparatory task, exception applies, and nothing about the claimant is evaluated, so no profiling. Minimal.

text: Finding 3 (low). Scope: the document-intake step for residence permits for medical treatment at the provincial migration office. Dossivane, a vision model trained by the supplier Haltwick Systems, labels each uploaded file as passport, hospital admission letter, proof of funds, insurance certificate or other, and files it in the applicant's dossier before an officer examines the application. We confirmed in the configuration and in twenty sampled dossiers that Dossivane reads no content beyond the document type, produces no assessment of the applicant and that officers see every file regardless of its label. The finding concerns retention only: mislabelled files are kept in a separate folder for 18 months without a documented reason. Recommendation: set and document a retention period for that folder.
rationale: A trained vision model in the examination of residence-permit applications (migration area) that only labels and files document types before an officer examines them: a preparatory task, exception applies, and no applicant is assessed, so no profiling. Minimal.

text: Hi Joris, following our call: the underwriting team wants Formleaf only for the attending physician's statements that come with life insurance applications. Formleaf's extraction model turns the doctor's free-text statement into our structured medical questionnaire (diagnoses with dates, current medication, smoking status, last blood pressure reading) and puts each value next to the sentence it came from. Our underwriters then do the rating exactly as today; Formleaf gives no rating, no loading and no accept/decline signal, and we will not connect it to the pricing engine. We need a data processing agreement, EU hosting and a test on 300 anonymised statements before go-live. Could you send the security questionnaire and the reference list by Friday? Best, Ilse
rationale: A learned extraction model in the risk assessment of life-insurance applicants (essential services, point 5(c)) that only structures the physician's statement for the underwriter, giving no rating or price: a preparatory task, exception applies, no evaluation of the applicant by the system, so no profiling. Minimal.

text: Q: Your platform says it only prepares the interview, so is anything automated about the candidate? A: Good question. Before each interview for a care-home post, Brightpanel reads the candidate's application and reference letters with its language model and produces a one-page preparation sheet for the panel: the questions to ask, the gaps in the work history, and an estimate of how reliable and how punctual the candidate is likely to be, based on what referees wrote. The panel makes the decision; Brightpanel never rejects anyone and never ranks the candidates. Q: Is the reliability estimate shown to the candidate? A: Not at the moment, but candidates can ask for their sheet. Q: Which languages? A: English, Dutch and German today.
rationale: A language model in recruitment for care posts (employment area) whose task is preparatory, so the exception would apply, but it estimates each candidate's reliability and punctuality: profiling, which cancels the exception. The preparation sheet is generated text.

text: The Kestrow Valley social welfare board will process applications for the home-help subsidy automatically from next month. Tollimber, a model trained on six years of past decisions, reads each application and the attached medical certificate, estimates the applicant's care needs and income situation, and grants the subsidy directly when its confidence is high. Applications it is less sure of, about one in five, go to a caseworker. The board expects decision times to fall from six weeks to three days. Applicants who are refused can ask for a review by a caseworker within thirty days. The board's chair said the change frees staff for home visits to the people with the most complex needs.
rationale: A trained model that decides eligibility for a public care subsidy (essential services, point 5(a)) by itself in most cases, replacing the human assessment, so no exception; it evaluates each applicant's care needs and income, which is profiling.

text: Risk R-17, online final examinations, nursing degree. System: Examsentry, supplied by Morrowfield Learning, which watches the candidate's screen activity, keystroke rhythm and network traffic during remote exams with an anomaly-detection model. The supplier describes it as preparatory, because an invigilator is meant to review each alert. In practice, since the spring sitting, candidates with three or more alerts are automatically scheduled for an in-person resit and their online result is withheld; invigilators review only the alerts candidates appeal against. Risk: candidates with assistive software or unstable connections are flagged more often. Owner: examinations officer. Current rating: high likelihood, medium impact. Action: restore invigilator review of every alert before any result is withheld; due before the winter sitting.
rationale: A learned anomaly detector that monitors candidates' behaviour during exams (education area); presented as preparatory, its alerts in fact withhold results and trigger resits without human review, so no exception; it evaluates each candidate's behaviour, which is profiling.

text: Background: Call-taking for out-of-hours medical help in the Saltmere region is under strain. Methods: We deployed Callmark, a speech and language model that listens to each incoming call, fills the structured call record and proposes one of four urgency levels, which the call handler sees highlighted and confirms with a single key. We compared 9,400 calls before and 10,100 after deployment. Results: median time to an urgency decision fell from 141 to 88 seconds. Handlers kept the proposed level in 96% of calls. Under-triage, judged by a panel against outcomes at 48 hours, did not change significantly. Conclusions: Proposed levels speed up call handling, but their near-universal acceptance means they effectively set the urgency of each call.
rationale: A learned model that evaluates incoming calls for medical help and proposes the urgency (essential services, point 5(d)); handlers accept it almost always, so it influences the decision and the exception does not apply; assessing each caller's medical urgency is profiling. It fills a record but does not converse.

text: Risqlet — the underwriting copilot for life and health insurers. Problem: medical underwriting takes 11 days on average because attending physicians' statements arrive as free text. Product: Risqlet's model reads the statement, structures it, and returns a suggested extra-mortality loading and a smoker/non-smoker class for each applicant, ready for the underwriter to apply. Traction: two mid-sized insurers in production; 64% of suggested loadings applied unchanged; time to offer down to three days. Business model: per-application fee, €4.10. Team: former chief underwriters and two machine-learning engineers from a reinsurance analytics group. Ask: €3.5M seed to add disability and critical-illness products and open an office in Milan. Contact: founders@risqlet.example
rationale: A learned model in risk assessment and pricing for life and health insurance (essential services, point 5(c)) that suggests the loading and class applied to each applicant, so it shapes the outcome and no exception applies; evaluating each applicant's health risk is profiling.

text: 4.3 Sling check and voice guidance. The Hoistwell 300 mobile patient lift, a class I medical device, carries load cells in each spreader-bar hook. During the first two seconds of every lift, a model trained on sensor recordings from correctly and incorrectly fitted slings compares the load distribution across the four hooks; if it detects a twisted strap or an unequal fit, it stops the lift and lowers the patient back onto the surface. The voice assistant then talks the carer through refitting the sling and answers questions such as "which loop goes on the left hook?" in plain language. The check does not replace the two-carer procedure described in section 3. Do not use the lift if the check indicator stays red after refitting.
rationale: A learned sling-fit check on a powered patient lift, stated as class I and consistent with MDR Rule 13 (an active device with no higher rule), so not high-risk through the product route; the voice assistant converses with carers and answers questions in its own words.

text: How Wrenfold House cut falls on outdoor walks. Wrenfold House's 140 residents use Ambrella rollators on the garden paths and for trips into town. The rollator, self-certified by its maker as a class I medical device, has a small camera under the handlebar and a model trained on thousands of kerbs, steps and slopes; when it detects a drop or a steep downhill stretch ahead, it applies the brakes gently and the handles vibrate. There is no app and no screen, and nothing is recorded once the walk is over. In the first six months, staff logged 11 near-falls on outdoor walks compared with 29 in the same months the year before. Residents said the vibrating handles felt less patronising than an alarm.
rationale: A trained vision model in a powered rollator stated as a class I device (MDR Rule 13), so not high-risk through the product route; it profiles nobody, does not converse and generates no content: minimal.

text: Product: Spinbay TS-9 sample sorter. Classification: in vitro diagnostic instrument, class A under the manufacturer's declaration of conformity. Intended purpose: to receive primary blood and urine tubes in the hospital laboratory, read their labels and cap colours, check sample integrity and sort the tubes into racks for the analysers. A convolutional model trained on 220,000 tube images detects haemolysed, clotted or under-filled samples and diverts them to a manual inspection rack; it gives no result about the patient's condition. Performance: 99.4% sensitivity for clotted samples against laboratory scientists' visual inspection. Users: trained laboratory staff. Changes in this submission: a new rack type and an updated image model with retrained weights.
rationale: A trained image model in an IVD instrument stated as class A, which maps to class I, so not high-risk through the product route; it checks sample quality rather than any person, does not converse and generates no content: minimal.

text: 2.2 Description of the processing. Quellstride is a powered walking frame for people living with dementia, placed on the market by Ottavell Mobility as a class I medical device. A camera on the frame films the user's face during walks, and a model classifies the expression as calm, anxious or distressed every few seconds. When distress persists for a minute, the frame slows down and sends an alert to the care team's phones. Purpose: earlier support for residents who become frightened while walking. Personal data: facial video frames (deleted after classification), the emotional-state labels and alert times, which are kept for 30 days. Recipients: the care team only. Legal basis: health care, with consent from each resident's legal representative.
rationale: A class I walking frame, so not high-risk through the product route, but the model recognises users' emotions from their faces: the biometrics area, with no exception because the classification is the system's main task; medical care, so not prohibited. Emotion recognition is set.

text: Note to file, pre-application meeting with Torvane Beds. The manufacturer asked whether adding a learned bed-exit predictor to its Ostrel electric ward bed changes the conformity route. The bed remains class I: an active device with no therapeutic function, and the new software runs inside the bed's controller. The predictor reads the four load cells under the mattress platform and, using a model trained on recorded movements, raises a nurse-call alert when the occupant's weight shifts in the way that typically precedes getting out of bed. It does not measure heart rate, breathing or any other physiological signal, and it stores no history beyond the current shift. We advised that the self-declaration route is unaffected and no notified body involvement is required.
rationale: A learned bed-exit predictor inside an electric ward bed that stays class I (an active device under MDR Rule 13, no physiological monitoring), so not high-risk through the product route; it detects movement without evaluating the person, does not converse and generates no content: minimal.

text: Chapter 7 — Lab assistant. The Pellcourt PX-2 automated pipetting station is an in vitro diagnostic instrument, class A. From firmware 3.0 it includes a lab assistant on the touchscreen: technicians type or speak questions such as "why did run 14 stop?" or "how do I recalibrate channel 3?", and a language model answers in full sentences, drawing on the instrument's error log and this manual. The assistant can also write a short summary of the day's runs for the shift handover. It cannot change protocols, volumes or calibration values; every change still needs a supervisor login. If an answer contradicts this manual, the manual takes precedence; report the answer through the feedback button so the supplier can review it.
rationale: An IVD instrument stated as class A, which maps to class I, so not high-risk through the product route; its language-model assistant converses with technicians and writes answers and summaries: limited.
